Where a manufacturer chart exists, air pressure and fork rebound come from it — matched to your weight. Temperature and weight only change values you haven\'t adjusted yourself: your own changes stay put. All other click values are starting points; the factory recommendation for your unit comes from the manufacturer (Fox: 4-digit ID on ridefox.com).
Search symptom — e.g. nervous, dives, bucks
More resistance to slow compression keeps the geometry stable.
The low-speed circuit carries pumping and cornering loads.
Buzzing hands, no grip on small stuff
More sensitive response in the first third of travel.
High speed means how fast the suspension moves, not how fast you ride.
Oil flows faster, the hit is absorbed instead of passed on.
Skips over root sections, never settles
The rear can\'t keep up with repeated hits.
Bobs when pedaling, sags under motor load
Motor torque acts like constant pedaling.
The spring gives its energy back too fast.
Slows fast extension after a hard hit.
Feels dead, stays low through repeated hits
The travel isn\'t there for the next obstacle.
Check sag, then add one volume spacer
Fox: once sag is right, volume spacers set bottom-out resistance. Only add air pressure as far as sag stays in the target range.
Preload is only for fine-tuning sag (Fox: max 2 turns) and doesn\'t replace spring rate.
Fox: if preload can\'t reach the sag, you need a different spring.
Front wheel lifts on steep climbs
Steeper seat angle, more weight over the front.
Bigger contact patch, the casing wraps around edges better.
Rear insert instead of more pressure
Rim contact. More pressure costs grip.
Suspension dull and sluggish in winter
Cold oil is thicker and damps more.
Set pressure again at riding temperature
Air pressure follows absolute temperature: at about 110 psi, 20 → 0 °C costs roughly 8 psi.

The number shows how many clicks the adjuster is open from its closed stop. 0 means fully closed.
To count: turn clockwise to the soft stop, never force it, then turn counter-clockwise and count the clicks.
Arrows show the turn direction at the dial. Plus and minus only change the number.
Shock preload ring: clockwise = more clicks = more preload = less sag.
Everything to the middle — that\'s your zero point
Rear spring rate, front air pressure
Measure sag, correct it, measure again
Changing the spring rate later means re-tuning everything. One change per ride.
Fork: push the O-ring against the seal, get off, measure the distance.
Shock (coil): eye-to-eye length unloaded and loaded, the difference is sag.
Always standing in the attack position, with your pack. Bounce a few times, then stand still. Measure two or three times.
Fox recommends 15–20 % sag on the fork and about 30 % on a coil shock — the fork deliberately runs less sag. That\'s normal.

In Setup you set the riding temperature (base 20 °C). Air pressure and tires then show the fill pressure at 20 °C that reaches the target at that temperature — if you pump up outside, take the target from the hint. Clicks follow the oil: cold = opened further, warm = closed further.
Cold oil damps more — winter and summer are 1–3 clicks apart
Air spring: about 4 % less pressure per 10 °C colder — at 110 psi, 20 → 0 °C is about 8 psi
A rear coil spring stays constant
1.8 bar at 20 °C is only about 1.6 bar at 0 °C
Check tire and fork pressure at riding temperature, not in the warm workshop. Never judge on a cold bike.

Prevent bottoming out. That\'s the job of volume spacers up front (with correct sag) and, on a coil shock, the spring rate — preload only fine-tunes sag. Closing HSC makes the suspension harsher on edges but doesn\'t replace progression.
The factory clicks for your unit aren\'t in the spec sheet. Enter the 4-digit ID on the fork leg or shock at ridefox.com — and note them here before you change anything.
Click counts from the manufacturer\'s manual — check them on your own bike.
Starts on this bike\'s fork, shock and spring — change them in Setup. Frame options (flip chip, dropper) stay off.

Manufacturer = statement by the manufacturer · Rule of thumb = common practice · Estimate = own estimate. The instructions of the respective component always take precedence.

Reminders about services that are due
Garden hose with a gentle spray, or a bucket and brush. Never a pressure washer: it forces water past bearing seals, into the motor and into the shock bushings.
Don\'t spray motor, bottom bracket or shock from below.
Cover the motor, display and charging port while washing.
Remove coarse dirt while it is still wet. Dried mud works like sandpaper.
Wipe the stanchions of fork and shock, then put a drop of Brunox Deo on the wipers.
Wipe the post\'s wiper too. One drop of Brunox Deo, cycle the post fully in and out a few times, wipe off the excess.
Clean it and lube it with e-bike chain oil. On an e-MTB it is the most heavily stressed wear part.
Dry it after wet rides and close the rubber cap.
Don\'t put it away wet in the basement. Let it dry first.
Dropper post in the seat tube
Never silicone or care spray. Silicone on the rotor means: the brake doesn\'t grab.
No penetrating oil. It flushes out the chain oil and doesn\'t lubricate by itself.
No penetrating oil and no Brunox. It thins the bearing grease. Bearings get grease during service.
Only products explicitly made for it. Ordinary sprays attack the wipers.

Preservative sprays are comfort, not protection. They delay flash rust and make cleaning easier. Against water in bearings, charging port and motor, what helps is a fender, proper washing technique, assembly paste and dry storage.
Underside of the down tube, top tube, right chainstay, seatstay, dropouts, head tube flanks. Degrease the frame first, apply the film wet with soapy water.
In addition to the film. The chain hits harder on a heavy e-MTB.
Keeps dirt off the shock eye, bushings and seat tube.
Keeps spray off the stanchions and wipers.
For stanchions only in mud. Remove it afterwards and let it dry, otherwise it becomes a damp chamber.
Outdoors only a breathable cover, no airtight tarp.
Apply to the dropper post, headset seat, axles, rotor bolts and motor mounts at delivery. This prevents aluminum and steel from seizing.
Protects from rain but not from condensation. The bike is wet in the morning without it having rained. Only for hours or one night, not as a permanent solution.
Rotors (flash rust), chain, steel spring, contacts and bearings.
Don\'t stand it directly on cold concrete. A stand creates distance.
In the workshop humidity matters more than temperature. A thermo-hygrometer shows within two weeks whether you have a problem.
Salty spray is the worst case for aluminum-steel contact points.
Leave it extended when the bike stands for a longer time. Don\'t lift the bike by the saddle with the post lowered.
Manufacturer statements in this section come from Bosch.
After the ride: wipe the battery dry.
Bring it indoors to charge and wait 1 to 2 hours until it reaches room temperature.
Charge only between 0 and 40 °C, ideally at room temperature.
Store at 30 to 60 % charge, cool, dry and frost-free.
In frost, insert the battery just before you set off.
Carry the spare AXS battery and spare coin cells warm in an inside pocket.
Do not charge. Charging forms lithium deposits, the capacity loss is permanent. Let it warm up first.
Allowed. Better to let it reach room temperature first: less condensation, gentler charging.
Good. Room temperature is ideal, roughly 15 to 20 °C.
Allowed. Right after the ride, let it cool for 15 to 30 minutes. Don\'t charge in the sun.
Do not charge. Let it cool down first.
Never warm up a cold battery on the radiator.
After the cold: how long to wait?
Wipe the charging port and contacts dry. Fogging shows there first.
At temperatures near or below 0 °C, wait longer until it no longer feels cold.
Cool, dry and frost-free, roughly 5 to 15 °C.
Do not store below −10 °C or above 60 °C.
Not recommended permanently below 0 °C. A single frosty night without charging does no acute harm.
Practically no difference from room temperature. The difference only counts over weeks and months.
During longer storage check the charge every 2 months. Top up if below 30 %.
Possible as long as it doesn\'t freeze. What counts is the overnight low, not the daily average. A min-max thermometer shows it.
Remove the battery. Cover the bay and charging port.
Only wipe battery contacts dry. No contact spray, no grease.
Roughly 5 to 10 % less usable capacity. The first range display is pessimistic and corrects itself after 10 to 15 minutes.
Plan for 20 to 30 % less range than in summer.
Insert the battery just before you set off, then take it back indoors.

An orange LED means the cell is low. To change it, unscrew the remote and pull out the rubber insert, which is the holder. The pairing is kept. Green blinking for 10 seconds means the cell is seated correctly.
Coin cells lose capacity but are not damaged. If a remote cuts out in the cold, the cell is due.
Put a CR1620 and a CR2032 in your pack.
Spare battery in the inside pocket. When storing, put the protective cap on the contacts. Do not charge below 0 °C.
The bearings themselves are standard parts. So are headset, wheels, crank, brakes, Fox suspension, SRAM and Bosch drive. The UDH mount is an industry standard and available everywhere.
Pivot bolts, sleeves and spacers, rocker link, flip-chip inserts, shock bushings, motor covers, battery mount.
The Pija has a replaceable, sealed cartridge. It is available as a spare part.
Keep a rear-triangle bearing set with bolts and sleeves, shock bushings and a spare flip chip in stock.
Saddle clamp at the post head 8 to 10 Nm, post clamp on the frame 7 Nm maximum.
Fox gives the hours as the maximum between two services.
Once after about 4 weeks or 300 km (Bosch)
First check by the dealer. After that, follow your dealer\'s guidelines.
With system diagnostics and software update. The dealer may set a different interval.
With a torque wrench to the manufacturer\'s spec. On a new bike, a lot settles.
Play check: rear triangle, headset, motor mount
Grab motor, rear triangle and headset by hand and wiggle them. Play at the motor mount is a known tolerance issue on Gen5 motors.
Clean the lowers, fresh oil, new wipers and foam rings.
Every 125 operating hours or 12 months, whichever comes first (Fox)
Lower-leg service, rebuild the damper, service the air spring.
Every 125 operating hours or 12 months, whichever comes first (Fox)
The air-can service (30 to 50 hours) applies only to air shocks, not to the DHX2 Coil.
Replace at 3 mm or less pad thickness including backing plate. After new pads and rotors, repeat the bedding-in.
Every 24 months (SRAM), more often with frequent riding or heavy braking
Mineral-oil brakes like the Maven. DOT brakes yearly. Use only the mineral oil specified by SRAM.
With the gauge. On 12-speed replace the chain at just 0.5 % stretch, otherwise it eats the cassette and chainring.
First after 6 months, then every 12 months
Check for play, disassemble and regrease if needed. Many manufacturers grease sparingly at the factory.
280 to 300 psi, 300 maximum. The valve sits under the top cap. Without a valve there is nothing to adjust.
Every 6 to 12 months, depending on use (ONOFF)
With heavy riding closer to 6 months. According to ONOFF the cartridge lasts up to 5 years.
Wipe the seat tube dry, apply fresh assembly paste. This prevents seizing.
Open the valve and check. There is often too little sealant from the factory.
Every 2 months, only for a stored battery
